documents.title: Post/Guild arbitration memo — claim deadline, Task Force on personnel practices
documents.subject: Notice to employees on filing arbitration claims by December 2, 1997; Guild representation and cost-sharing; non-retaliation; Personnel Practices Task Force to be formed January 1998 under Director of Personnel Carl Williams
documents.date: 1997 (approx.; references December 2, 1997 deadline and January 1998 task force)
documents.notes: Clean typewritten narrative page, no heading visible — appears to be a continuation page of a two-part Post/Guild arbitration agreement announcement (per the attached selected answer). Page bottom is cut off mid-sentence at "volunteer their".

pages.transcript:
Claims must be filed by December 2, 1997. Claim forms
and a copy of the arbitration procedures are available from the
Personnel Department (202-334-7174) or the Guild (202-393-0808).
Anyone considering filing a claim should examine the claim form
and the arbitration procedures carefully. They contain important
information concerning such matters as: the kinds of claims that
will be considered, the information that should be provided to
pursue a claim, the steps that the arbitrator will follow in
resolving a claim, the party's options with respect to
representation, and the payment of the costs and fees of the
arbitrator. The Guild will provide representation to anyone who
requests it, in which case the Guild will pay the claimant's
share (50%) of the arbitrator's fee and costs.
          Consistent with its general policy and with the
requirements of law, the Post will not retaliate against any
employee who participates in an arbitration proceeding.
     *     The agreement calls for the establishment of a
Task Force to examine personnel practices for Guild-covered
positions in the commercial departments. The Task Force, to be
formed in January 1998, will look at such issues as hiring,
promotion, training, communications, diversity, career
development and performance evaluation. It will be chaired and
appointed by the Director of Personnel, Carl Williams, and will
include at least 15 employees from the commercial departments, no
more than half of whom will be supervisors or managers. All

documents.title: Post employee-survey responses on race/gender and advancement (page 4)
documents.subject: Two-column printed page of responding employees' quoted statements (demographic descriptor + comments) on hiring, promotion, and discrimination at The Washington Post
documents.notes: Newspaper/bulletin-style two-column layout, page numbered 4. Left edge of the left column is torn/obscured by a paper curl, so the opening words of the first three paragraphs are lost. Content matches the questionnaire-response style seen elsewhere in the collection.

pages.transcript:
[LEFT COLUMN — top three entries have their leading words torn away]

...think that on the basis of selectivity, I think they are very
[..]ve in the National staff quality, but not selective enough on
metro staff.

... The Post could do a better job in hiring better qualified mi
nority reporters. They don't put enough effort in recruiting qual
fied ones, and just want to fill a slot. So they hire very young
and
inexperienced minorities. A self-fulfilling prophecy.

White male, six years or more, 30 years old or younger, Style/
News Desk/Sports/Editorial/Other, Reporter:
     I think that The Post has deficiencies in its dealing with mino
rities, but management has tried over the years to improve.

White male, five years or less, 30 years old or younger, Nation
al/Financial/Investigative/Foreign, Reporter:
     I feel that you should be asking more about not only blacks, but
Hispanics as well.

White male, Editor:
     The questionnaire offered no measure of the effectiveness of
The Post's actual hiring, let alone recruiting, of minorities. Last
showed great promise at every turn — especially in free-lancing
several pieces for the Weekly, assigned to test his writing ability.
The process of interviews and consideration was lengthy, and in
the end no job worth (illegible) considered. He had, nevertheless, several
years of writing and editing for Time-Life Books. The Evening
Sun hired me as a editorial writer and he now does a weekly col
umn as well.

White female, Metro, Reporter:
     They should hire the best qualified people regardless of race or
sex. Promotion should be based solely on ability. I think it does
more of an injustice to black readership to have unqualified blacks
reporting than having a lower component of black reporters. Also,
there are a lot of qualified black reporters around the country, and
if you're going to fill numerical quotas, they should screen and
look for highly experienced black reporters and editors.

White female, National/Financial/Investigative/Foreign, Report
-er:
     I'd like to see more women in management.

White female, Metro, Reporter:
     It would be a better local newspaper if there were more black
reporters. Black reporters are sought after unfairly to do inner
city stories, but at the same time they might do better in those
type of stories because of their experience with black people by
their being black.

White male, National/Financial/Investigative/Foreign, Reporter:
     In this city, The Post should have many more black reporters,
and I believe we can get them without compromising quality one
bit.
     I am more concerned, in terms of discrimination, with instances
of woman being denied opportunities for advancement on the ed
-iting track.

[RIGHT COLUMN]

     I believe the hiring and advancement of women and blacks at
The Post do not become a significant problem until it reaches
the AME level.

White male, Style/News Desk/Sports/Editorial/Other, Reporter:
     Apart from recruitment and promotion policies, which no doubt
could be substantially improved in an institutional sort of way, the
only question I would raise about the culture in the newsroom is
whether there is a kind of intellectual segregation here, bred be
cause it is "easier" for white editors not to cultivate generalism in
black reporters as they do in whites. That is, everyone seems
black reporters as they do in blacks, "stick to" issues of race relations,
most comfortable when blacks "stick to" issues of race relations,
urban life and development, black politics, and poverty. A risk-tak
ing company would strongly encourage blacks to break out of
these obvious reporting slots and develop the breadth of experi
ence that would make them strong candidates for promotion.
There's nothing wrong with blacks covering blacks — often it
may even be crucially important. The only losers under that ar
rangement are the blacks reporters looking for advancement — I
don't know, maybe they see it that way.

White female, Style/News Desk/Sports/Editorial/Other, Editor:
     I cannot comment accurately on the hiring policies of The Post
regarding blacks and women. I can clearly comment on the num
ber of AMEs who are blacks or women. One suggestion for an in
stant survey: take the last 20 notices that have been posted in the
main bulletin board in which a new appointment was more men
tioned: my bet would be that a widely high number of those an
nouncements have concerned white men. Another suggestion:
look around the main newsroom, not the Style newsroom, and
count the number of blacks or women in glass-in offices. One fi
nal suggestion: count the number of women and the advances
ments that have been made for women at The Post (the women's
discrimination suit in 1972 (I think) and representation for women is better — or worse — than it was when the wo
men won the discrimination suit.

White male, Style/News Desk/Sports/Editorial/Other, Reporter:
     I have the uncomfortable feeling that Washington Post manage
ment is trying to do something other than to be the best damn
paper in the world.

White female, National/Financial/Investigative/Foreign, Editor:
     If you're going to hold positions open for minorities, you must
have the aggressive recruitment to match! We've had a vacancy
for several months because apparently we can't find a qualified
minority editor to fill it — and we all are suffering — and morale
is slipping — because the position has gone unfilled! It is absurd
that a paper with the resources and prestige of The Post can't
seek to find an applicant for month(s). It just makes us all feel man
agement A) doesn't care or B) is insincere in efforts to promote
blacks. If you don't care enough to fill it — please let us fill it with
a qualified, dedicated part-timer, no matter what race or sex.

White female, Metro, Reporter:
     It was hard to do some of this survey because I honestly believ
The Post has done a lot to try to hire and promote more blacks and I
just don't think it's done them in the right way — especially in it
initial hiring operations.
     So when I give negative ratings it's not because I think the pro
gram hasn't tried or should do more. It should just do it different
     Make better hires and pay attention to them. That's good
service for ALL personnel operations.
